parts.latex: The graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{3}x^3-4x^2-9x+5$ has a local maximum turning point at:

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and find the stationary points.

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= x^2-8x-9\\ &= (x-9)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$

So $y'=0$ at $x=-1$ and $x=9$.

The second derivative decides the nature.

$$y''=2x-8$$

At $x=-1$, $y''=-10<0$, so there is a local maximum.

The $y$-value there is

$$\begin{aligned} y &= -\dfrac{1}{3}-4+9+5\\ &= 9\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

The local maximum is at $\left(-1,\ 9\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$, which is option A.

solutions.latex:
The factors $(x-2)^2$ and $(x+2)^2$ are never negative.

So the sign of $x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2$ is the sign of $x$, except where a squared factor is zero.

$$\begin{aligned} x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2 &> 0 &&\text{for } x>0, x\neq 2\\ x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2 &= 0 &&\text{for } x=-2,\ 0,\ 2\\ x(x-2)^2(x+2)^2 &< 0 &&\text{for } x<0, x\neq -2 \end{aligned}$$

Hence the expression is $\ge 0$ for $x\ge 0$ and at $x=-2$.

This is option A.

parts.latex:
A ball thrown upwards from a building attains a height above the ground given by the function $h(t)=8t-2t^2+12$, where $t$ is the time in seconds and $h$ is in metres.

Find the value for $t$ for which $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=0$ and hence find the maximum height above the ground the ball reaches.

solutions.latex:
The maximum height occurs where $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 8-4t = 0\\ t &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

Test the nature with the second derivative.

$$\dfrac{d^2h}{dt^2}=-4<0$$

So the graph is concave down and this is a maximum.

$$\begin{aligned} h(2) &= 8(2)-2(2)^2+12\\ &= 20 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ t=2 \text{ and the maximum height is } 20 \text{ m}$$

parts.latex: Find the first and second derivative of the function $f(x)=(x^2-4)^3$.

solutions.latex:
Use the chain rule for the first derivative.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3(x^2-4)^2\times 2x\\ &= 6x(x^2-4)^2 \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=6x & v&=(x^2-4)^2\\ u'&=6 & v'&=4x(x^2-4)\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= 6(x^2-4)^2+6x\times 4x(x^2-4)\\ &= 6(x^2-4)\left[(x^2-4)+4x^2\right]\\ &= 6(x^2-4)(5x^2-4) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f'(x)=6x(x^2-4)^2 \text{ and } f''(x)=6(x^2-4)(5x^2-4)$$
criteria: Finds $f'(x)$ and applies the product rule for $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit

3889.stem: Lucy contemplates playing a new game which involves tossing three coins simultaneously. She will receive \$10 if she obtains 3 heads, \$5 if she obtains 2 heads and \$3.00 if she obtains 1 head. However, if she obtains no heads, she must pay \$20. She must also pay \$5 for each game she plays.

parts.latex: What is Lucy's expected gain?
Is this a fair game? Why?

solutions.latex:
The gain $X$ for 0, 1, 2, 3 heads, with each probability from three tosses, is:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} X & -20 & 3 & 5 & 10\\ \hline P(X) & \dfrac{1}{8} & \dfrac{3}{8} & \dfrac{3}{8} & \dfrac{1}{8}\end{array}$$

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= -20\times\dfrac{1}{8}+3\times\dfrac{3}{8}+5\times\dfrac{3}{8}+10\times\dfrac{1}{8}\\ &= \$1.75 \end{aligned}$$

This is before the \$5 fee.

$$\therefore\ E(X)=\$1.75$$

meta.format_note: Source's expected value of \$1.75 is before the \$5 fee; part (b) uses the fee.

solutions.latex:
It costs \$5 to play, so the expected gain per game is

$$\begin{aligned} 1.75-5 &= -3.25 \end{aligned}$$

Lucy can expect to lose \$3.25 per game on average.

A fair game has an expected gain of 0.

$$\therefore\ \text{It is not a fair game, as Lucy loses money.}$$

Consider the cone with a slant side of 9 cm below.

\exfigure{154_q9d_1}

figures.cap: cone with slant side 9 cm, height and radius

parts.latex: If the height is $x$ cm, show that the radius, $r$, is $\sqrt{81-x^2}$.
Show that the volume of the cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(81x-x^3\right)$.
Hence, find the height of the cone when the volume is maximum.

solutions.latex:
The cone's height, radius and slant side form a right-angled triangle.

By Pythagoras' theorem, with slant side 9 and height $x$:

$$\begin{aligned} r^2+x^2 &= 9^2\\ r^2 &= 81-x^2 \end{aligned}$$

Since $r>0$,

$$\therefore\ r=\sqrt{81-x^2}$$

The volume of a cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$, with $h=x$ and $r^2=81-x^2$.

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(81-x^2)x\\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(81x-x^3\right) \end{aligned}$$

Expand and differentiate.

$$\begin{aligned} V &= 27\pi x-\dfrac{1}{3}\pi x^3\\ \dfrac{dV}{dx} &= 27\pi-\pi x^2 \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$.

$$x^2=27$$

Since $x>0$, $x=\sqrt{27}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.

$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-2\pi x=-2\pi\sqrt{27}<0$$

So this is a maximum.

$$\therefore\ \text{the height for maximum volume is } \sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}$$

$$\therefore\ F(x)=(x-1)^2$$

parts.latex:

\extable{154_q10c_t1}
Find the expected value of $X$.
Find $P(X<\mu)$.

solutions.latex:
Substitute each value of $x$ into $P(X=x)=\dfrac{x^2}{30}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4\\ \hline P(X=x) & \dfrac{1}{30} & \dfrac{4}{30} & \dfrac{9}{30} & \dfrac{16}{30}\end{array}$$

The expected value is $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 1\times\dfrac{1}{30}+2\times\dfrac{4}{30}+3\times\dfrac{9}{30}+4\times\dfrac{16}{30}\\ &= \dfrac{100}{30}\\ &= 3\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$

From part (b), $\mu=\dfrac{100}{30}=3\dfrac{1}{3}$, so $X<\mu$ means $X=1,2,3$.
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(X<3\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{30}+\dfrac{4}{30}+\dfrac{9}{30}\\ &=\dfrac{14}{30}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{15} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X<\mu)=\dfrac{7}{15}$$

parts.latex: If the radius of the base is $x$ cm, show that the volume is $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(300x-\pi x^3\right)$ cm$^3$.

solutions.latex:
Let the height be $h$ cm. The volume of a cylinder is
$$V=\pi x^2h \quad (1)$$
The can is open, so the surface area is the base plus the curved surface.
$$300=\pi x^2+2\pi xh$$
Hence
$$2\pi xh=300-\pi x^2$$
$$h=\dfrac{1}{2\pi x}\left(300-\pi x^2\right) \quad (2)$$
Substitute (2) into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\pi x^2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\pi x}\left(300-\pi x^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{x}{2}\left(300-\pi x^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(300x-\pi x^3\right) \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

Writes the surface area equation, or equivalent merit

$$V=150x-\dfrac{1}{2}\pi x^3$$

$$\pi x^2=100$$

So this is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3000}{\sqrt{\pi}}-\dfrac{1000}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1000}{\sqrt{\pi}} \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

3902.stem: The cost of running a train at a constant speed $v$ km/h is $C=50+\dfrac{v^2}{100}$ dollars per hour.

parts.latex: Find the time taken for an 800 km journey in terms of $v$.
Hence, find an expression for the cost of an 800 km journey.
Find the most economical speed for this journey.

solutions.latex:
Use speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$.
$$v=\dfrac{800}{t}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{800}{v} \text{ hours}$$

The cost of the journey is the cost per hour multiplied by the time.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost}&=\left(50+\dfrac{v^2}{100}\right)\times\dfrac{800}{v}\\ &=\dfrac{40000}{v}+8v \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the product of cost per hour and time, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the cost with respect to $v$.
$$\text{Cost}=40000v^{-1}+8v$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dv}(\text{Cost})=-40000v^{-2}+8$$
Set the derivative to zero.
$$v^2=5000$$
Since $v>0$,
$$v=\sqrt{5000}\approx 70.71 \text{ km/h}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2}{dv^2}(\text{Cost})=\dfrac{80000}{v^3}>0 \text{ for } v>0$$
So this is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the most economical speed is about } 70.71 \text{ km/h}$$
criteria: Solves for $v$ and tests for a minimum, or equivalent merit

3903.stem:
Janet is a biologist completing research on bee hives on the river called \textit{Bend}. The river follows the curve $y=x^2-1,\ x\ge 0$ as shown below. All lengths are measured in kilometres.

Janet's research station is located at $(0,0)$ and the Bee hive ($P$) is located at $(0,1)$.

Janet was interested in a Bee hive ($R$) located on the \textit{Bend} river.

\exfigure{154_q13b_1}

figures.cap: curve y=x^2-1 with bee hives P(0,1) and R(s,t), research station at origin

parts.latex:
Using the distance formula, if the bee hive is at the point $R\ (s,t)$ show that the length ($L$) in kilometres in a straight line from $P$ to the bee hive located at $R$ is given by

$L=\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}$.

$\left[\text{Distance formula: }\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\right]$

If the Bee hive ($R$) is located at a point closet to the beehive ($P$).

Find $\dfrac{dL}{ds}$ and hence find the coordinates of the Bee hive ($R$).
Find the length ($L$), in kilometres, the direct line between the Bee hives.

solutions.latex:
$R$ lies on $y=x^2-1$, so $t=s^2-1$ and $R=(s,s^2-1)$.

Use the distance formula between $P(0,1)$ and $R$.
$$\begin{aligned} L&=\sqrt{(s-0)^2+\left((s^2-1)-1\right)^2}\\ &=\sqrt{s^2+(s^2-2)^2}\\ &=\sqrt{s^2+s^4-4s^2+4}\\ &=\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the coordinates of $R$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} L&=(s^4-3s^2+4)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ \dfrac{dL}{ds}&=\dfrac{4s^3-6s}{2\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}}\\ &=\dfrac{2s^3-3s}{\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}} \end{aligned}$$
The denominator is positive, so $\dfrac{dL}{ds}=0$ when the numerator is zero.
$$s(2s^2-3)=0$$
Since $s>0$,
$$s=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$$
Then
$$t=\dfrac{3}{2}-1=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
Test the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} s=1:\ \dfrac{dL}{ds}&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}<0 &&\text{decreasing}\\ s=2:\ \dfrac{dL}{ds}&=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{8}}>0 &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Solutions of $-e^x(x+1)=x^2-1$ are the intersections of $y=-e^x(x+1)$ with the parabola $y=x^2-1$.

Both pass through $(-1,0)$ and $(0,-1)$, since $x^2-1=0$ at $x=-1$ and $x^2-1=-1$ at $x=0$.

So $x=-1$ and $x=0$ are solutions. We check there are no others by comparing the two sides on each interval.

For $x>0$: $e^x\ge 1+x$, so $-e^x(x+1)\le-(x+1)^2$, and
$$-(x+1)^2-(x^2-1)=-2x(x+1)<0$$
so the exponential curve is below the parabola: no solution.

For $x<-1$: put $t=-x>1$. The equation $e^{-t}(t-1)=(t-1)(t+1)$ needs $e^{-t}=t+1$, impossible since $e^{-t}<1<t+1$: no solution.

For $-1<x<0$: divide by $x+1>0$ to get $-e^x=x-1$, that is $e^x+x-1=0$. The function $e^x+x-1$ is increasing and equals $0$ only at $x=0$, so there is no solution in this interval.

Therefore there are exactly $2$ solutions, option B.

A surveyor who is $y$ metres due south of a tower sees the top of it with an angle of elevation $8^\circ$.

A second surveyor is $x$ metres due east of the tower.

From her position the angle of elevation is $10^\circ$ to the top of the tower.

parts.note: 3D trigonometry (two surveyors and a tower): now Year 11 Extension 1.

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle formed by the tower (height $h$), the base and the surveyor, the angle of elevation is $8^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 8^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{y}\\ y&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}\end{aligned}$$

Similarly, for the second surveyor, $x=\dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ}$.

The surveyors and the base of the tower form a right-angled triangle (right angle at the base), so by Pythagoras' theorem
$$x^2+y^2=940^2$$
Substitute.
$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ}\right)^2&=940^2\\ h^2\left(\cot^28^\circ+\cot^210^\circ\right)&=940^2\\ h&=\sqrt{\dfrac{940^2}{\cot^28^\circ+\cot^210^\circ}}\\ &\approx 103.3\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
The height of the tower is $103$ m, to the nearest metre.

Estimate $D$ by using the trapezoidal rule with 4 sub-intervals.

Give your answer current to the nearest centimetre.

solutions.latex:
The distance is the integral of the rate, so $D=\displaystyle\int_1^5A(t)\,dt$.

With 4 sub-intervals, $h=\dfrac{5-1}{4}=1$, so the function values are needed at $t=1,2,3,4,5$.

$$D\approx53.4277685$$

$$\therefore\ D\approx53 \text{ cm}$$

3962.stem: A function is given by $f(x) = 4x^2 - x^4$.

parts.latex: By solving $f(x) = 0$ show that $x$-intercepts are $-2$, 0 and 2.
Prove that $f(x)$ is an even function.
Show that $f'\left(\sqrt{2}\right) = 0$.
Given that $\left(\sqrt{2},4\right)$ is a maximum turning point, explain in words why $\left(-\sqrt{2},4\right)$ is also a maximum turning point.

solutions.latex:
Solve $f(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 4x^2-x^4&=0 \\ x^2(4-x^2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x^2=0$ or $4-x^2=0$.

$$\therefore\ x=0 \text{ or } x=\pm2$$

A function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=4(-x)^2-(-x)^4 \\ &=4x^2-x^4 \\ &=f(x) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is an even function}$$

Differentiate term by term.

$$f'(x)=8x-4x^3$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'\left(\sqrt2\right)&=8\sqrt2-4\left(\sqrt2\right)^3 \\ &=8\sqrt2-4\times2\sqrt2 \\ &=0 \end{aligned}$$

Since $f$ is even, its graph is a reflection of itself in the $y$-axis.

So every stationary point on the right of the $y$-axis has a matching stationary point of the same type on the left.

$$\therefore\ \left(-\sqrt2,4\right) \text{ is also a maximum turning point}$$

A city is suffering through a drought and adopts a plan to import water from another city.

It is given that the volume of water imported in the $1^{\text{st}}$ year since the start of the plan is $1.8\times10^{9}\ \text{m}^3$. In subsequent years, the volume of water imported each year is 90% of the volume of water imported in the previous year

Find how much water was imported in the $4^{\text{th}}$ year.

Give your answer correct 1 decimal place.

Find the total volume of water imported in the first 10 years.

Give your answer correct 1 decimal place.
Explain why the total volume of water imported since the start of the plan will never exceed $1.9\times10^{10}\ \text{m}^3$.

solutions.latex:
The yearly volumes form a geometric sequence with $a=1.8\times10^9$, $r=0.9$ and $n=4$.

$$\begin{aligned} T_4&=ar^{n-1} \\ &=1.8\times10^9\times0.9^{3} \\ &\approx1.3\times10^9 \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$

The total is the sum of the first 10 terms of the geometric sequence, $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$, with $a=1.8\times10^9$, $r=0.9$, $n=10$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{10}&=\dfrac{1.8\times10^9\left(0.9^{10}-1\right)}{0.9-1} \\ &=1.172378808\times10^{10} \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ S_{10}\approx1.2\times10^{10} \text{ m}^3 \text{ (1 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Correct value of $S_{10}$ before rounding, or equivalent merit
Correct sum formula substitution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $|r|=0.9<1$, the series has a limiting sum.

$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{1.8\times10^9}{1-0.9} \\ &=1.8\times10^{10} \end{aligned}$$

The total can never exceed $1.8\times10^{10}$, and $1.8\times10^{10}<1.9\times10^{10}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the total never exceeds } 1.9\times10^{10} \text{ m}^3$$

parts.latex: Solve $e^{2\ln x} = 4x + 21$

So $x=7$ or $x=-3$.

$$\therefore\ x=7$$

3966.stem: The displacement of an object measured in metres after $t$ seconds is given by $x = e^{t^2} - 2t^2$.

parts.latex: Given that the velocity is the rate of change of the displacement, find an expression for the velocity.
Find the two times when the object is stationary.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement.

$$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(e^{t^2}-2t^2\right)$$

$$v=2te^{t^2}-4t$$
criteria: Differentiates one term correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The object is stationary when $v=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2te^{t^2}-4t&=0 \\ 2t\left(e^{t^2}-2\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $t=0$ or $e^{t^2}=2$.

$$\begin{aligned} e^{t^2}&=2 \\ t^2&=\ln2 \\ t&=\pm\sqrt{\ln2} \end{aligned}$$

Time cannot be negative, so $t\ge0$ and $t=-\sqrt{\ln2}$ is rejected.

$$\therefore\ t=0 \text{ s or } t=\sqrt{\ln2} \text{ s}$$
criteria: Solves one factor and finds both candidate times, or equivalent merit

Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Differentiate $2te^{t^2}$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uw)=u'w+uw'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=2t & w&=e^{t^2} \\ u'&=2 & w'&=2te^{t^2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} a&=2e^{t^2}+2t\times2te^{t^2}-4 \\ &=2e^{t^2}+4t^2e^{t^2}-4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the area is given by $A = 3x\sqrt{9-x}$.
Find the value of $x$ that will maximise the area, showing why this is the maximum.

solutions.latex:
The fencing covers the side $x$ and the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is $18-x$ m.

In the right-angled triangle, the side along the wall $h$ satisfies Pythagoras' theorem.

$$\begin{aligned} h&=\sqrt{(18-x)^2-x^2} \\ &=\sqrt{324-36x} \\ &=\sqrt{36(9-x)} \\ &=6\sqrt{9-x} \end{aligned}$$

The area is half base times height.

$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac12\times x\times6\sqrt{9-x} \\ &=3x\sqrt{9-x} \end{aligned}$$

Write $A=3x(9-x)^{\frac12}$ and use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x & v&=(9-x)^{\frac12} \\ u'&=3 & v'&=-\dfrac12(9-x)^{-\frac12} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx}&=3(9-x)^{\frac12}-\dfrac{3x}{2}(9-x)^{-\frac12} \\ &=\dfrac{6(9-x)-3x}{2\sqrt{9-x}} \\ &=\dfrac{54-9x}{2\sqrt{9-x}} \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 54-9x&=0 \\ x&=6 \end{aligned}$$

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side of $x=6$; the denominator is positive for $x<9$, so the numerator $54-9x$ decides the sign.

\extable{Ts5767_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $x=6$ gives a maximum.

Alternatively, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{-9(12-x)}{4(9-x)^{\frac32}}$, and at $x=6$ this is approximately $-2.598<0$, so a maximum.

$$\therefore\ x=6 \text{ m}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following pairs of transformations commute?

solutions.latex:
Two transformations commute when applying them in either order gives the same result. Test each pair on a point $(x,y)$.

Option C: reflection in the $y$-axis is $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)$ and reflection in the $x$-axis is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$.
$$(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y) \qquad (x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$$
The results are the same in either order, so these commute.

The other pairs do not commute. For a vertical reflection and a vertical translation by $k$:
$$\text{reflect then translate: } -y+k \qquad \text{translate then reflect: } -(y+k)=-y-k$$
For a vertical translation by $k$ and a vertical dilation by factor $2$:
$$\text{translate then dilate: } 2(y+k) \qquad \text{dilate then translate: } 2y+k$$
A horizontal translation and a horizontal dilation fail in the same way.

So the correct option is C.

so $1+3+5+\cdots+\ell=225$, an arithmetic series with $a=1$, $d=2$.

The last term is
$$\begin{aligned} \ell&=a+(n-1)d \\ &=1+(n-1)\times 2 \\ &=2n-1 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
For a given arithmetic sequence, the ratio of the sum of the first $m$ terms to the sum of first $n$ terms is $m^2:n^2$, where $m\neq n$.

solutions.latex:
The ratio of the sums of the first $m$ and $n$ terms, using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$, is
$$\dfrac{\frac{m}{2}\left(2a+(m-1)d\right)}{\frac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)}=\dfrac{m^2}{n^2}$$
Cancelling $\dfrac{m}{n}$ on both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2a+(m-1)d}{2a+(n-1)d}&=\dfrac{m}{n} \\ 2an+mnd-nd&=2am+mnd-md \\ 2an-2am&=nd-md \\ 2a(n-m)&=d(n-m) \end{aligned}$$
Since $m\ne n$, we may divide by $n-m$:
$$d=2a \qquad (1)$$
The ratio of the $m^{th}$ to the $n^{th}$ term is, using (1),
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a+(m-1)d}{a+(n-1)d}&=\dfrac{a+(m-1)2a}{a+(n-1)2a} \\ &=\dfrac{1+2(m-1)}{1+2(n-1)} \\ &=\dfrac{1+2m-2}{1+2n-2} \\ &=\dfrac{2m-1}{2n-1} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T_m:T_n=(2m-1):(2n-1)$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $y = \ln\dfrac{x\left(x^2-1\right)}{x+1}$.

$$\therefore\ P = 2.5\%$$

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int \cos x^{\circ}\,dx$

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \dfrac{x}{2x^2+1}\,dx$

parts.latex:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and leave each answer as a single simplified fraction:

$y=(3x-4)\sqrt{5-2x}$

solutions.latex:
Write $y = (3x-4)(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 3x - 4 & v &= (5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ u' &= 3 & v' &= -(5-2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}} - \dfrac{3x-4}{(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}} \\ &= \dfrac{3(5-2x) - (3x-4)}{\sqrt{5-2x}} \\ &= \dfrac{19 - 9x}{\sqrt{5-2x}} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= \sin x & v &= 1 + \cos x \\ u' &= \cos x & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{(1+\cos x)\cos x - \sin x(-\sin x)}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x + \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x + 1}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1+\cos x} \end{aligned}$$

4038.stem: Jasmine's salary in her job increases by the same amount every year. In the $4^{\text{th}}$ year at her job she earned \$81 000. In the $9^{\text{th}}$ year of her job she earned \$98 500.

Bree started a job at the same time, and with the same starting salary as Jasmine. Bree's salary, however, increased by 2% per annum. With the use of logarithms, show in which year will her income first be greater than \$100 000?

solutions.latex:
The salary forms an arithmetic sequence with first term $a$ and common difference $d$, so $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} a + 3d &= 81\,000 \\ a + 8d &= 98\,500 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting:
$$\begin{aligned} 5d &= 17\,500 \\ d &= 3500 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} a + 10\,500 &= 81\,000 \\ a &= 70\,500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{first year pay is } \$70\,500 \text{, with an annual increase of } \$3500$$

meta.format_note: Fixed the id: part (a) working had $T_4$ and $T_9$ equations unchanged.

solutions.latex:
Use the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n-1)d\right)$, with $n = 15$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left(2\times 70\,500 + 14\times 3500\right) \\ &= \$1\,425\,000 \end{aligned}$$

Bree's salary is a geometric sequence with $a = 70\,500$ and $r = 1.02$, so $T_n = 70\,500(1.02)^{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 70\,500(1.02)^{n-1} &> 100\,000 \\ 1.02^{n-1} &> \dfrac{200}{141} \end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms of both sides (the base $1.02>1$, so the inequality is unchanged):
$$\begin{aligned} n - 1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{200}{141}\right)}{\log 1.02} \\ n - 1 &> 17.65\ldots \\ n &> 18.65\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ she first earns more than $\$100\,000$ in her 19th year at the job.
criteria: Uses logarithms to solve for $n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin\theta}-\tan\theta=\sec\theta$

solutions.latex:
Express $\tan\theta$ as $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ and use a common denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin\theta} - \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta - \sin\theta(1-\sin\theta)}{(1-\sin\theta)\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sec\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes over a common denominator, or equivalent merit

4043.stem:
A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\le t\le 14\\[2mm] 0 & \text{for } 0\le t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$
After how many days will a person have a 75% chance of showing symptoms after they have contracted the virus?

solutions.latex:
The total probability over the domain is 1.
$$\int_1^{14} \dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k}{2}\int_1^{14} \dfrac{2}{2t-1}\,dt &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{14} &= 1 \\ k\left(\ln 27 - \ln 1\right) &= 2 \\ k\ln 27 &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k = \dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$$
criteria: Sets the total area equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $T$ days be the time at which the cumulative probability is 0.75.
$$\int_1^{T} \dfrac{\frac{2}{\ln 27}}{2t-1}\,dt = \dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\ln 27}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{T} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ \ln(2T-1) &= \dfrac{3\ln 27}{4} \\ 2T - 1 &= e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} \\ T &= \dfrac{e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} + 1}{2} \\ &\approx 6.4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after 7 days}$$
criteria: Sets up the integral equal to 0.75, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\sqrt{\dfrac{2+x}{2-x}}\right]=\dfrac{2}{4-x^2}$

solutions.latex:
Use the log laws to rewrite the function, then differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{2+x}{2-x}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right] &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2+x)-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2-x)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2+x}+\dfrac{1}{2-x}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2-x+2+x}{(2+x)(2-x)}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{4}{4-x^2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{2}{4-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

4046.stem: A drug is used to control a medical condition. It is known that the quantity $Q$ milligrams of drug remaining in the body after $t$ hours satisfies an equation of the form $Q=Q_0e^{kt}$ where $Q_0$ and $k$ are constants. The initial dose is 6 milligrams and after 15 hours the amount remaining in the body is half the initial dose.

parts.latex: Find the values of $Q_0$ and $k$.
After how long will one-eighth of the initial dose remain?

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$, $Q=Q_0$, so $Q_0=6$.

After 15 hours the amount is half the initial dose, so $Q=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 6e^{15k} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= e^{15k} \\ 15k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$k = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{15}$$

One-eighth of the initial dose is $\dfrac{6}{8}=\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4} &= 6e^{kt} \\ \dfrac{1}{8} &= e^{kt} \\ kt &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $k$ from part (a).
$$t = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\div 15} = 45 \text{ hours}$$
criteria: Sets up equation for one-eighth of the dose, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Kloe has taken up golf, each year she plays 30 rounds of golf. In 2011 she totalled 3300 shots, in 2021 she totalled 2760 shots. The number of shots she took each year decreased by the same amount. To make it as a professional golfer she needs to get under 2115 shots in her 30 rounds. If this trend continues, in what year can she become a professional golfer?

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} a+10d &= 2760 \\ 10d &= -540 \\ d &= -54 \end{aligned}$$
She needs fewer than 2115 shots.
$$\begin{aligned} a+(n-1)d &< 2115 \\ 3300+54-54n &< 2115 \\ -54n &< -1239 \\ n &> 22.944\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So $n=23$ years, and Kloe can be a professional golfer in 2033.
criteria: Finds the common difference, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the derivative of $y=\log_e(\tan x)$ is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\tan x+\cot x$

which is the required result.

The tangent is

Now $2.4 \text{ m}=240 \text{ cm}<250 \text{ cm}$.

parts.latex: Simultaneously solve the equations $\log_{10}(2-x)-\log_{10}y=1-\log_{10}2$ and $\log_{10}2x=\log_{10}y$

4056.stem: The acceleration of a particle is given by $\ddot{x}=4\cos 2t$, where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially the particle is at the origin with a velocity of 1 ms$^{-1}$.

parts.latex: Show that the velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$
Find the time when the particle first comes to rest.
Find the displacement, $x$, of the particle in terms of $t$.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$\dot{x}=\displaystyle\int 4\cos 2t\,dt=2\sin 2t+C$$
When $t=0$, $\dot{x}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 2\sin 0+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin 2t+1 &= 0 \\ \sin 2t &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The first time $2t>0$ with $\sin 2t=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ is in the third quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned} 2t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

Integrate the velocity.
$$x=\displaystyle\int(2\sin 2t+1)\,dt=-\cos 2t+t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$.

parts.latex: If $y = \dfrac{x}{\ln x}$, show that $y^2 - xy + x^2 y' = 0$
